title: Johnson's Plan to Push Voter ID Bill Through Congress Without Democrats Clears Key Hurdle
excerpt: The SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register for federal elections, advances via budget reconciliation — a move with direct implications for naturalized citizens.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Speaker Mike Johnson's SAVE America Act advances without Democratic support, clearing a key House committee vote.
  • The bill requires documentary proof of citizenship for federal election registration, impacting millions of naturalized citizens.
  • The reconciliation package proposes $95 billion in federal spending over ten years for various initiatives.
  • Critics label the legislation as 'Jim Crow 2.0,' arguing it creates barriers for eligible voters.
  • A final House vote on the reconciliation bill is expected by Wednesday afternoon.
  • Speaker Mike Johnson's plan to embed the SAVE America Act into a budget reconciliation bill survived a key House Rules Committee vote on Monday, bypassing the need for Democratic support in the Senate.
  • The SAVE Act would require documentary proof of US citizenship to register for federal elections, a measure that could affect naturalized citizens, including millions of Indian Americans.
  • The reconciliation bill would authorize $95 billion in new federal spending over 10 years, covering election integrity funding, military replenishment amid the Iran war, and farm aid.
  • Democrats have called the legislation "Jim Crow 2.0," arguing it would create barriers for eligible voters. A final House vote is expected by Wednesday.

House Speaker Mike Johnson's strategy to advance a controversial voter identification bill without Democratic support cleared a critical hurdle on Monday evening, bringing the legislation one step closer to a full House vote expected later this week.

The Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act, which would require documentary proof of US citizenship to register for federal elections, has passed the House but stalled in the Senate, where Democrats have blocked it from reaching the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome a filibuster.

The Reconciliation Gambit

Johnson's solution is to fold key elements of the SAVE Act into a larger budget reconciliation bill — a legislative mechanism that allows the party in power to pass fiscal legislation with a simple majority in both chambers, bypassing the Senate filibuster entirely.

https://x.com/Bubblebathgirl/status/2079235321263423922

The House Rules Committee approved the framework on Monday, setting the stage for a floor vote on the procedural rule Tuesday afternoon and a final vote on Wednesday at 3:30 p.m., according to a schedule obtained by Fox News.

The reconciliation package would authorize $95 billion in new federal spending over the next decade, encompassing election integrity funding, military replenishment amid the ongoing US war with Iran, and aid to American farmers.

What the SAVE Act Would Require

The legislation would amend the National Voter Registration Act to require documentary proof of US citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections. Acceptable documents would include a valid US passport, certain REAL ID-compliant identification indicating citizenship, or military identification with records showing a US birthplace.

Supporters argue the bill addresses election integrity concerns by ensuring only citizens can register. Critics counter that non-citizen voting is already illegal under federal law and that the new requirements would create unnecessary barriers for eligible voters who lack easy access to citizenship documents.

Why Indian Americans Should Watch

For the estimated 5.4 million Indian Americans in the United States, many of whom are naturalized citizens, the SAVE Act carries direct implications. Naturalized citizens would need to present documentary proof of citizenship — such as a naturalization certificate or US passport — to register, adding a step that native-born citizens with standard state identification would not face.

Implications for Indian Americans
›5.4 million Indian Americans in the U.S. may be affected.
›Naturalized citizens must provide proof of citizenship to register.
›Older immigrants and recent citizens may face additional burdens.
›Civil rights groups warn of a two-tiered registration process.

While most Indian Americans likely possess the required documents, the additional burden could disproportionately affect older immigrants, recent citizens, or those whose naturalization paperwork is not readily accessible. Civil rights organizations have warned that any proof-of-citizenship requirement risks creating a two-tiered registration process.

The Political Battle

President Trump has thrown his full support behind the measure, urging Republicans to advance it as part of the reconciliation bill. "Get AS MUCH of THE SAVE AMERICA ACT as possible in a Budget Bill, along with aid to our incredible Farmers, and funding for our Military," Trump posted on social media Monday.

Democrats have fiercely opposed the bill. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has repeatedly called it "Jim Crow 2.0," arguing that "the goal of the SAVE Act is the same: disenfranchising American citizens and making it harder for eligible people to vote, particularly low-income Americans and people of color."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries accused Republicans of prioritizing "voter suppression legislation" over housing, healthcare, and grocery costs.

What's Next

Even if the reconciliation framework passes the House this week, it sets only the broad spending parameters. The relevant committees would then draft the specific legislative details — including exactly which SAVE Act provisions make it into the final bill — before stitching everything back into a single package for passage through both chambers.

Some Republican senators, including Thom Tillis, have warned they may oppose the SAVE Act provisions if they survive to the Senate version. The bill's fate in its current form remains uncertain, but its advancement through reconciliation represents the most viable path yet for the legislation Trump has called his "number one priority."
